title: Turn repeated questions into better reply drafts | Workflow Lab
description: An original Workflow Lab walkthrough. Test with fictional data and review results before connecting live customer systems. Narration uses a local synthetic voice.
slides: Answering the same customer question again? Build a reply draft workflow before automating the send button.
Create a short reference document with your service area, opening hours, and approved answers. Leave out customer information.
Ask your AI tool: Draft a reply using only this reference. If a fact is missing, ask me instead of guessing.
Test it with a question about pricing that your reference does not answer. A useful draft should admit it needs details.
Check every draft before sending. When customers keep asking the same thing, improve the reference rather than adding another prompt.

title: A simple estimate follow-up system | Workflow Lab
description: An original Workflow Lab walkthrough. Test with fictional data and review results before connecting live customer systems. Narration uses a local synthetic voice.
slides: An estimate follow-up does not need a complicated sales system. Start with one spreadsheet and a useful next step.
Use columns for customer, estimate date, status, last contact, and next follow-up date. Keep personal details in your approved system.
Filter for open estimates with a next follow-up date before today. Exclude declined work and anyone who opted out.
Draft a short message: Do you have questions about the estimate? I can explain the scope or help with timing.
Review the recipient and message, send through your normal channel, and update the last contact date. Track replies, not just messages sent.

title: Make AI summarize tasks without inventing deadlines | Workflow Lab
description: An original Workflow Lab walkthrough. Test with fictional data and review results before connecting live customer systems. Narration uses a local synthetic voice.
slides: An AI summary can sound organized while quietly inventing a deadline. Use a stricter task extraction prompt.
With a non-confidential sample, ask: Extract each action, its owner, and its deadline. Quote the sentence that supports each field.
Add this rule: If an owner or date is missing, write not specified. Do not infer it from context.
Compare the extracted list with the original notes. A phrase like soon is not a calendar date.
Only move verified tasks into your tracker. The time saver is finding commitments faster, while you still decide what gets assigned.

title: Check a spreadsheet before trusting the dashboard | Workflow Lab
description: An original Workflow Lab walkthrough. Test with fictional data and review results before connecting live customer systems. Narration uses a local synthetic voice.
slides: Your dashboard can be wrong even when every formula works. Check the source rows before building another chart.
Start with three checks: Is each record unique? Are required fields filled? Are dates stored consistently?
Keep a stable record identifier. Two customers with the same name are not automatically duplicate records.
Compare your row count and total amount with the original export. Investigate any difference before deleting or changing rows.
Keep the raw export unchanged and clean a copy. A small validation tab makes next month easier to check.

title: Build a useful AI prompt with a test case | Workflow Lab
description: An original Workflow Lab walkthrough. Test with fictional data and review results before connecting live customer systems. Narration uses a local synthetic voice.
slides: A reusable AI prompt needs a test case, not just more instructions. Try this with a service description.
Write the task: Rewrite this description for a customer. Then specify the audience, tone, and maximum length.
Add boundaries: Use only facts in the input. Keep prices unchanged. Do not invent guarantees or qualifications.
Now test it with a description that has no price. The output should not create one just to sound complete.
Save the prompt alongside that test input and an acceptable output. Recheck both when you change the instructions.

title: Name your files so automation can find them | Workflow Lab
description: An original Workflow Lab walkthrough. Test with fictional data and review results before connecting live customer systems. Narration uses a local synthetic voice.
slides: Before connecting another app, fix the file names your workflow relies on. Predictable inputs make simpler automations.
Pick a pattern such as year, month, day, project, and document type. Use a consistent date format like four-digit year first.
Keep a stable project identifier when names can change. Avoid putting sensitive customer information in a shared filename.
Test the pattern on five real examples, including a revised document. Decide how you will label revisions before moving files.
Try the rule in a test folder first. Keep a record of old and new names so a mistake is easy to undo.

title: Use a dry run before an automation sends anything | Workflow Lab
description: An original Workflow Lab walkthrough. Test with fictional data and review results before connecting live customer systems. Narration uses a local synthetic voice.
slides: The most useful automation setting is often a dry run. It shows what would happen before anything is sent.
For a follow-up workflow, create a preview with the intended recipient, draft message, and reason the row was selected.
Use fictional test records for an open estimate, a declined estimate, and a customer who opted out.
Check that only the open estimate appears in the preview. Also test a missing email address and a repeated record.
Keep sending disabled until those cases behave correctly. After launch, retain a simple activity log and an easy off switch.

title: Make a small business checklist that stays useful | Workflow Lab
description: An original Workflow Lab walkthrough. Test with fictional data and review results before connecting live customer systems. Narration uses a local synthetic voice.
slides: A checklist should prevent a missed step, not become another document nobody reads. Start with one repeated task.
Write the trigger at the top. For example: Use this checklist when a new service request arrives.
List observable actions: Confirm the address, record the requested work, and tell the customer when to expect a response.
Put the exception beside the step it affects. If the address is outside your service area, route it for review.
Test the checklist on your next three requests. Remove vague steps, add missing decisions, and assign someone to keep it current.
